lesson.title: Both at Once: Codominance and Roan Cattle
lesson.summary: Codominance produces offspring in which both alleles are fully and separately expressed at the same time, not merged into a new blended color the way incomplete dominance blends traits.
lesson.body:
Codominance is another exception to simple dominance, and it is easy to confuse with incomplete dominance because both involve a heterozygote that does not simply look like the dominant homozygote. The mechanisms are different, though. Incomplete dominance blends two traits into a new, diluted intermediate, such as pink from red and white. Codominance does not blend anything, both alleles are expressed fully and distinctly, side by side, in the same individual.

Coat color in cattle illustrates the difference well. A red coat allele, R, and a white coat allele, W, are codominant with each other. RR cattle are solid red, WW cattle are solid white, and RW cattle are roan, a coat made up of individual red hairs and individual white hairs growing side by side across the body. There is no diluted pink hair anywhere on a roan animal, both original colors are simply present at once, patch by patch and hair by hair.

Working through the cross confirms the same underlying math as incomplete dominance, even though the biology differs. Cross two roan cattle, RW by RW. Each parent produces R and W gametes in equal proportion, giving offspring in a ratio of one quarter RR, red, one half RW, roan, and one quarter WW, white. The genotype and phenotype ratios line up one to two to one, just as they did for the pink snapdragons, but here the middle class is roan because of literal co-expression of both colors, not a new blended shade.

The most medically important example of codominance in humans involves the ABO blood group, where the A and B alleles are codominant with each other, so a person carrying both displays both the A and B antigens on their red blood cells at once. That system also involves a third allele beyond just A and B, which is enough of a wrinkle that it gets its own full treatment in the next chapter on multiple alleles.
